issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must plead and prove performance, or continuous readiness and willingness to perform, the essential terms required of the claimant.
material_facts: The claim sought specific performance of an alleged agreement to sell, under which part of the price had been paid and the balance was payable when the sale deed was executed and registered.

The plaint referred to the agreement, the payment, a later notice asking the seller to obtain permission and execute the sale deed, and the seller’s failure to do so, but did not suggest that the claimant had performed or was continuously ready and willing to perform his own obligations.

The claimant’s testimony principally addressed the existence and validity of the agreement and the parties’ dealings, and did not categorically assert performance or continuous readiness and willingness.

The opposing party’s written statement did not raise the absence of the required averment, but the claimant did not establish readiness and willingness through the pleadings and evidence considered as a whole.
issues.conclusion: Specific performance was properly refused because the claimant failed to aver and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as applicable to the suit, specific performance could not be enforced for a claimant who failed to aver and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms required of that claimant, except terms whose performance was prevented or waived by the other party. The required averment did not demand a particular formula, but its substance had to appear in the plaint; the whole pleadings and evidence, and the claimant’s conduct, had to be assessed. The opposing party’s failure to object did not remove the claimant’s burden. The Court relied on Umabai v. Nilkanth Dhondiba Chavan (2005) 6 SCC 243; A. Kanthamani v. Nasreen Ahmed (2017) 4 SCC 654; Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty (1999) 6 SCC 337; and Aniglase Yohannan v. Ramlatha (2005) 7 SCC 534, including the requirements reflected in Forms 47 and 48 of Appendix A to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.readiness_not_pleaded: The claimant did not plead in substance that the claimant had performed or was continuously ready and willing to perform the essential obligations required of the claimant.
predicates.readiness_not_proven: The claimant’s evidence and conduct, considered with the whole record, did not establish performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential obligations required of the claimant.

issues.definition: In a suit for specific performance, if the claimant omits the required substantive pleading or fails to establish performance or continuous readiness and willingness, the relief is denied.

issues.legal_issue: A court may reject an appellate-stage amendment that attempts belatedly to cure the absence of a substantive readiness-and-willingness case in a suit for specific performance.
material_facts: The claimant sought leave to amend the plaint only after the opposing party challenged the trial decree on the ground that the plaint lacked the required readiness-and-willingness averment.
The amendment application was made at the appellate stage and sought to add an averment about readiness and willingness.
The claimant had not established readiness and willingness in the original pleadings and evidence, and the proposed amendment would have attempted to fill that gap at a late stage.
issues.conclusion: The appellate courts committed no illegality in refusing the belated amendment; in the circumstances, the attempt to improve the pleadings at the appellate stage was futile.
issues.legal_principle: The substantive requirement under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 could not be reduced to a matter of form, and adding the phraseology of readiness and willingness at a late stage did not cure the failure to plead and prove the substance of the claim. The Court also applied Sections 100 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 to the scope of the second appeal concerning the refusal of amendment.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.amendment_sought_at_appellate_stage: The claimant sought an amendment only after the matter had reached an appellate stage.
predicates.amendment_would_fill_substantive_lacuna: The proposed amendment sought to add a substantive part of the claimant’s case that had not been pleaded or established earlier.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a specific-performance suit seeks an appellate-stage amendment to supply a missing substantive part of the case, the amendment may be rejected as belated.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a second appeal may consider an additional substantial question of law only after recording reasons for doing so, and the power is reserved for exceptional cases supported by strong and convincing reasons.
material_facts: The second appeal was admitted on two formulated substantial questions of law, neither of which concerned the refusal of the amendment application.

The High Court did not formulate an additional substantial question concerning the refusal of amendment and did not record strong and convincing reasons for hearing the appeal on such an additional question.
The appellant argued that the High Court could have considered the amendment issue under the proviso to Section 100(5) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not at fault for declining to consider the challenge to the amendment refusal, because no substantial question of law on that issue had been formulated and there were no strong and convincing reasons to formulate and hear an additional question.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 100 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 require a second appeal to proceed on a substantial question of law formulated by the High Court. The proviso to Section 100(5) permits the High Court to hear an additional substantial question not previously formulated only after recording reasons, and does not displace the other requirements of Section 100; the power is for exceptional cases and requires strong and convincing reasons. The Court relied on Surat Singh (Dead) v. Siri Bhagwan (2018) 4 SCC 562.

rule.if: second_appeal and additional_question_not_formulated and not strong_reasons_recorded

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal before a High Court.
predicates.additional_question_not_formulated: The substantial question of law at issue was not formulated for the second appeal.
predicates.strong_reasons_recorded: The High Court recorded strong and convincing reasons for hearing the appeal on that additional substantial question of law.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, an unformulated substantial question is not heard where the High Court has not recorded strong and convincing reasons to consider it.
